name: Main Central Road

timeline.event: First laid out as a main road of the old Travancore kingdom
The 47 km Chengannur–Ettumanoor stretch is rebuilt and widened by Kerala PWD

history: The Main Central Road, or MC Road, is one of Kerala's oldest and most important highways. It was first laid out more than two centuries ago, when the region was ruled by the kingdom of Travancore, and it was literally the kingdom's central road — the spine that tied the capital to the inland towns. Kerala has two natural north–south corridors: a coastal one and an inland one just below the hills, and the MC Road is the inland one. It links Thiruvananthapuram with a chain of busy market towns — Kottarakkara, Adoor, Chengannur, Thiruvalla, Changanassery, Kottayam, Muvattupuzha and Perumbavoor — before ending at Angamaly near Kochi. Today it is numbered State Highway 1 and is maintained by the Kerala Public Works Department. Even though it is mostly a two-lane road, it carries a huge amount of traffic, because in this part of Kerala the towns almost run into one another.
facts: Kerala's State Highway 1 — the number 1 marks it as the state's most important state highway.
About 240 km long, from Kesavadasapuram in Thiruvananthapuram to Angamaly.
Its starting point, Kesavadasapuram, is named after Raja Kesavadas, a famous Dewan (chief minister) of Travancore.
Crosses six districts: Thiruvananthapuram, Kollam, Pathanamthitta, Alappuzha, Kottayam and Ernakulam.
Serves as the main inland alternative to the coastal NH 66 through central Kerala.
Kalady, near its northern end, is the birthplace of the philosopher Adi Shankaracharya.
It carries very heavy pilgrim traffic in the Sabarimala season from November to January, when buses pour through Chengannur and Kottayam.
Unlike most long Indian highways it has no ghat or mountain section — it stays in Kerala's gently rolling midland belt the whole way.
significance: For millions of people in central Kerala this is simply the road. It is how you get to the district hospital, the college, the market and the bus stand, and it is the route most inter-district buses take. It also matters far beyond Kerala during the Sabarimala pilgrimage season, when hundreds of thousands of pilgrims from across south India travel along it toward Chengannur and Erumeli. Because it runs inland, it is the state's fall-back north–south route whenever the coastal NH 66 is blocked or flooded.

travelNotes: Do not judge this road by its length. Because it threads through town after town with shops opening straight onto it, the full 241 km usually takes six to seven hours, not three. Traffic is heaviest around Kottayam, Thiruvalla and Muvattupuzha, and during the Sabarimala season from November to January. There is no toll. The monsoon months of June to September bring heavy rain and occasional flooding around the Pamba and Periyar rivers; the driest and easiest months are December to March. Tea shops and toddy shops line the route, so food and fuel are never far away.
